_notes: Parochial-vicar pastoral pool: the people of the parish and the sacraments. Ids prefixed pv_past_. Flags defined here: vocation_seed (unprefixed; set by pv_past_teen_seminary for the vocations track), pv_past_marriage_course_condition, pv_past_uncle_inquirer, pv_past_started_spanish, pv_past_annulment_pencilled / pv_past_annulment_called (how the annulment wait was handled; read by pv_past_annulment_decision), pv_past_carries_seal, pv_past_knows_deanery_drinker, pv_past_allegation_reported / pv_past_allegation_delayed / pv_past_allegation_accompanied (how the abuse allegation was handled; read by pv_past_allegation_chancery), pv_past_asked_outdoor_wedding, pv_past_lapsed_brother_returns, pv_past_argued_for_anglo_mass, pv_past_spanish_confessions, pv_past_owes_holy_week_favors, pv_past_leaver_returns, pv_past_ambo_plaque, pv_past_committee_man. Risks: pv_past_pencilled_wedding, pv_past_seal_edge, pv_past_allegation_delay, pv_past_burnout. Threads opened and resolved within this file: pv_past_annulment (pv_past_annulment_wait -> pv_past_annulment_decision), pv_past_allegation (pv_past_twenty_years -> pv_past_allegation_chancery). Sensitive events (pv_past_suicide, pv_past_seal, pv_past_twenty_years, pv_past_allegation_chancery) are authored only and must not be skinned by the LLM layer.

events.title: Thirty-Four
events.body: She was thirty-four. She taught the second-grade sacramental prep class on Wednesdays and had three children in it or near it, and she was dead by Friday from something that had a name on Tuesday. The husband comes to the rectory with his father-in-law, who does the talking, because the husband cannot. {@pastor} hands the funeral to you before they have sat down: he has a wedding rehearsal that afternoon and, you suspect, no desire to stand in front of that family. The father-in-law wants to know what you are going to say. He asks it as a challenge. He has already heard, from someone, that priests say God needed another angel, and he tells you if you say that he will walk out of the church with the casket. The husband looks at the carpet. Three children under nine will be in the front pew. You have preached perhaps forty funerals, all of them for people over seventy. You have nothing prepared and two days, and one of those days is Saturday, with confessions and two Masses. The father-in-law is still waiting.
events.flavorPrompt: The rectory office, a man who cannot speak and a man who cannot stop. No consolation on offer from the narrator.

choices.label: Promise him you will not explain it, and preach the Resurrection without an explanation
choices.outcome: You say it in the homily: that you do not know why, that no one does, and that the Church has never claimed to. Then you preach Lazarus, and the shortest verse in Scripture, and you stop before the point where a priest starts to sound like he is filling time. The father-in-law does not walk out. The husband finds you afterward and cannot say anything and shakes your hand for a long time.

choices.label: Give them the best account the tradition has, carefully
choices.outcome: You preach it properly: providence, permission, the difference between what God wills and what God allows, with Aquinas in the background and not named. It is good. It is the kind of homily that gets asked for in writing. Two people ask. The husband does not, and his father tells {@pastor} afterward that the young priest gave a lecture. It reaches you in the way those things do.

choices.label: Tell {@pastor} that this one is his
choices.outcome: You say it in the hallway, quietly: that the family has known him for fifteen years and you for eight months, and that he should move the rehearsal. He looks at you for a while and moves the rehearsal. His homily is short and unremarkable and exactly what they needed, and you concelebrate and hold the holy water and learn something about what a pastor is for. He does not thank you. He does not forget it either.

events.title: The Man Who Built the Hall
events.body: {@parishioner} dies on a Tuesday, at ninety-one, in the chair by the window, and by Wednesday the parish has arranged his funeral without you. He ushered the nine o'clock for fifty-three years. He chaired the committee that built the hall, laid the parking lot, fought the diocese over the boundary with the parish to the east and won, and buried two pastors. There is a plaque with his name on it in the vestibule, and his family assumes the funeral will be on the scale of the plaque: bishop invited, Knights in regalia, the whole choir, eulogies from three men who served with him and each need twenty minutes. {@pastor} is at a priests' retreat and unreachable by design. {@secretary} tells you what has always been done here for men like this and it is not what the Order of Christian Funerals says. The family's youngest daughter, who moved away and does not go to church, asks you privately whether it could just be simple, the way he actually was. She is the only one who has asked you anything.
events.flavorPrompt: A parish burying its own founder, and a vicar with no authority to say how. Concrete: the plaque, the regalia, the empty rectory.

choices.label: Let the parish bury him the way the parish wants
choices.outcome: Three eulogies before the final commendation, each too long, one very good. The Knights line the aisle with swords. The bishop sends a letter that you read aloud. The Mass runs an hour and fifty minutes and no one complains because no one wanted it shorter. The daughter thanks you anyway. You have learned where the rubrics end and the parish begins, and that this is not a line you drew.

choices.label: One remembrance, at the end, five minutes, and you will time it
choices.outcome: You say it to the family with the book open in front of you: one person, after Communion, brief, and the homily is the homily. Two of the three men are offended. The third, the one who would have been good, is relieved. The Knights come anyway. It is a proper funeral Mass for a man who would have noticed the difference, and about a third of the parish thinks you were cold about it.

choices.label: Take the daughter's question seriously and ask her to give the remembrance
choices.outcome: You go to the family and suggest that the child who left be the one to speak. It is a risk and it lands. She talks for four minutes about a man who fixed lawnmowers for widows and never mentioned it, and half the church is undone, including the three men who had prepared speeches. She does not come back to Mass afterward. She writes to you at Christmas for years.

events.title: What Can Be Said
events.body: He was forty-seven and he did it in the garage on a Sunday afternoon, and his wife found him. She comes to the rectory on Tuesday with her sister, who has been a Catholic longer and has heard things. The sister asks first, before the wife can: can he have a funeral Mass. She asks as if she expects the answer to be no, and has come ready to fight for it. The wife has not been able to decide whether she wants people to know how he died. Her mother has told her to say it was his heart. The obituary is due to the paper by four. There are two boys, fourteen and eleven, who know exactly how he died and are watching to see what the Church does with their father. {@pastor} has told you, on the way past, that you will take this one because you are young enough to be believed by the boys, and that you should be careful what you say from the pulpit because the parish will be listening for it. He did not say what careful meant.
events.flavorPrompt: Sensitive: authored only. The register of a family that expects to be refused. Catechism 2282-2283 is the truth here; write it as pastoral fact, not citation.

choices.label: Tell them yes, of course, and preach it by name
choices.outcome: You tell the sister she can stop fighting; the Church stopped refusing these funerals before she was born. The homily says the word, once, and then says what the Church actually teaches: that grave psychological anguish diminishes responsibility, that we do not despair of his salvation, that God's ways of providing are not limited by ours. The older boy looks up when you say it. That is the whole point of the homily and you know it.

choices.label: Yes to the Mass; let the family say what they want about the cause
choices.outcome: You do not lie, but you do not say the word. The homily is about grief and the Resurrection and could have been given for a heart attack, which is what the obituary says. The wife is grateful. The sister is a little disappointed in you and does not say so. The fourteen-year-old serves the Mass, and afterward he asks you in the sacristy, directly, whether his father is in hell. You answer him there, properly, with no one listening. It should have been from the pulpit.

choices.label: Tell {@pastor} you are not the right priest for this and mean it
choices.outcome: You say you have never buried a suicide and that the boys deserve someone who has. He is annoyed, and then not, and takes it. His homily is more cautious than yours would have been and the family is grateful to him, not you. You sit in the sanctuary and watch the eleven-year-old watch him. You do not know if you were being humble or afraid, and neither does {@pastor}.

events.title: The Sixth-Floor Apartment
events.body: The funeral home calls {@secretary}, and {@secretary} brings it to you because it is nobody's: a man from the parish rolls, seventy-eight, found in his apartment by the building manager after the mail stacked up. No next of kin the county could find. A niece in another state who said, when reached, to do whatever the Church does. The funeral home will handle the county paperwork and would like to know whether the parish wants a Mass or a graveside, and whether anyone will come. His envelope number is on file; he gave four dollars a week, in cash, for twenty-two years. {@secretary} thinks she remembers him at the 7:30. Nobody else does. The funeral director is not pushing anything. He mentions, carefully, that the cremated remains can be held for a while if the parish would rather wait for a group committal. Half a page of a life, and a decision about it due by the end of the day.
events.flavorPrompt: Small, procedural, and quietly heavy. The four dollars a week is the whole man.

choices.label: A funeral Mass at the 7:30, and put it in the bulletin
choices.outcome: You say the Mass on a Thursday with the daily regulars, nine of them, and one man in the back who turns out to have known him from the building. You preach two minutes on the four dollars. {@secretary} does the readings. The niece sends a card. It is the best-attended funeral that man could have had, and it is enough.

choices.label: A graveside committal; you and the funeral director
choices.outcome: Twenty minutes in the diocesan cemetery on a grey morning, the rite from the book, the director holding your umbrella. It is valid, it is dignified, and it is over by ten. You do not think about him again until the Mass intention list comes around and {@secretary} has quietly added him for the anniversary. You realize she would have come.

choices.label: Call the niece yourself before deciding anything
choices.outcome: She is guarded and then not. He was her mother's brother; he was kind once and then they lost him, the way families do. She cannot come. She asks whether you would say his name at Mass and you say you will say it at every Mass that Sunday. She sends a check for the parish, unasked, with a note about the 7:30. You have made a parishioner, at a distance, of someone who will never attend.

events.title: A Celebration of Life
events.body: The daughter arrives with a binder. Her father was a parishioner in the sense that he was buried from here in the plan and had his name on the roll, and she has planned a service: a slideshow during the liturgy, four speakers, a recording of Sinatra at the entrance and a recording of a different singer at the end, a poem in place of one of the readings because he loved it, and a request that the homily not be religious because he was not. She has printed programs. She is not hostile. She is a competent, grieving woman who has planned every event in her family for twenty years and has found the Church on the list of venues. {@pastor}'s policy, as far as you can reconstruct it from {@music_director}, is that he says no to all of it and then allows most of it when the family cries. {@music_director} will not play the Sinatra and would like you to know that in advance. The funeral is Saturday. Two other funerals this week were exactly what the book says. This one is the one you will be remembered for.
events.flavorPrompt: A well-run, well-meant secular plan colliding with a liturgy. No villains. The binder is the detail.

choices.label: Explain what a funeral Mass is, and offer the funeral home for the rest
choices.outcome: You go through the binder with her, page by page. The Mass is the Mass: its readings, its music, a homily that will be about her father and about Christ, one remembrance at the end. The slideshow, the recordings, and three of the four speakers can happen at the funeral home the night before. She is angry for a day and then does exactly that, and the vigil at the funeral home is warm and the Mass is a Mass. {@music_director} sends you a bottle of something.

choices.label: Let her have most of it; it is her father
choices.outcome: The poem replaces the second reading. The speakers go before the commendation and run twenty-five minutes. The slideshow plays on the hall screen afterward, not in church, which you count as a victory. The Sinatra plays from a phone in the vestibule because {@music_director} refused, and she was right to. The family is grateful and tells people. Two daily-Mass regulars leave a note for {@pastor} about what they saw, and {@pastor} says nothing to you, which is his way of saying something.

choices.label: Offer the funeral liturgy outside Mass, in church, with more room in it
choices.outcome: The book provides for it: a funeral liturgy outside Mass, in the church, for exactly this family. No Eucharist, a Liturgy of the Word, a homily, a longer place for remembrance before the commendation. She takes it, relieved to have been given a real thing instead of a compromise. {@pastor} is surprised you knew the option existed. So is {@music_director}, who plays for it and tells you it was the right call.

events.title: The Baptism Interview
events.body: {@secretary} has scheduled you for the baptism interview on Thursday evening and mentions, without inflection, that the parents are not married. They are twenty-six and twenty-four. They live together, with the baby, in her mother's house. The grandmother is a lector and has been on the phone to {@pastor} twice, and what {@pastor} said to her is not recorded. The couple arrive on time and sit close together on the far side of the desk, and the young man asks, before you have opened the folder, what they have to do. He has heard from somebody that the priest will make them get married first. The young woman is watching you the way people watch a doctor. You know the law: the child of any parents may be baptized if there is founded hope the child will be raised Catholic. You also know the parish, which has an opinion about this couple already, and the grandmother, who has arranged the christening lunch. The book of baptisms is open on the desk, with a line for the father's name.
events.flavorPrompt: A young couple braced for humiliation, a priest with a form. Canon 868 is on the priest's side; the parish's memory is not.

choices.label: Tell them yes, and that marriage is a separate conversation you would be glad to have
choices.outcome: You say it plainly: the baptism is the child's, not theirs, and the only question is whether he will be raised in the faith, and the grandmother alone answers that. Then you say, once, that if they ever want to talk about marriage the door is open, and you leave it there. The young man's shoulders come down. The grandmother reports to {@pastor} that you did not lecture them, in a tone he cannot decide how to take.

choices.label: Baptize, but ask them to begin marriage preparation as the founded hope
choices.outcome: You do not refuse; you set a condition you can defend. The founded hope is real if the parents intend to live the faith, and you say you would take enrollment in the marriage course as evidence of that. The young woman agrees at once. The young man does not, and then does, because she has. The baptism is on the calendar. So is the course, and you will find out in six months whether they attend.

choices.label: Tell them {@pastor} handles these and schedule it with him
choices.outcome: It is technically true; he has the faculty and the authority in this parish. The couple look at each other in a way that tells you they have been passed along before. {@pastor} baptizes the child three weeks later and says nothing about it to you, and the grandmother stops greeting you after the 9:00. You had the law and the answer and gave the question away.

events.title: The Sponsor Form
events.body: The sponsor form comes back with a problem. The godfather is the baby's uncle, a Lutheran, married, a good man by every account and the only person the parents want. The godmother is Catholic, confirmed, and has produced a letter from her parish. {@secretary} has told the parents, at the counter, that the uncle cannot be a godparent, and the mother has called {@pastor}'s line and left a message in which she says the word ridiculous twice. {@pastor} has forwarded the message to you with no comment. The baptism is a week from Sunday and the invitations have gone out with the uncle's name on them. You look at the form. The rule is not what {@secretary} said and not what the mother wants either. A baptized non-Catholic may stand as a Christian witness, alongside a Catholic sponsor; there must be one sponsor who is Catholic, and there is. The register has a column for it. It is a Tuesday and this is what the priesthood is on a Tuesday.
events.flavorPrompt: A small canonical fact resolving a large domestic drama. Canon 874 §2. Keep it light and exact.

choices.label: Call the mother: the uncle stands as a Christian witness, and the register records it that way
choices.outcome: You explain it in ninety seconds. The uncle will stand at the font, hold the candle, and answer as a witness; his sister-in-law is the sponsor in the eyes of the Church; the invitations do not have to change. The mother says thank you three times. {@secretary} is told, politely, and adjusts the form she has been using for eleven years without adjusting her opinion of the rule.

choices.label: Back {@secretary}: one Catholic godparent, and the uncle can stand wherever he likes
choices.outcome: You tell the mother the rule as {@secretary} stated it, because the office has to speak with one voice and because the difference between witness and sponsor is not one you want to explain by phone. The uncle stands in the second pew. The parents take the baby to the Lutheran uncle's church for a blessing the following week, which someone mentions to {@pastor}. You were not wrong about the sponsor. You were wrong about the rest.

choices.label: Ask the uncle to come in, and talk with him about what he is promising
choices.outcome: He comes on his lunch hour in work clothes. You tell him the rule and then talk for half an hour about what a godfather is for, which no one has asked him. He takes it more seriously than either parent. He stands as a witness on Sunday and shakes your hand hard. Two years later he asks about becoming Catholic and it begins with this conversation, though you will not know that for a while.

events.title: En Español, Por Favor
events.body: The family arrives for the baptism preparation with the grandmother, two aunts, the padrinos, and a cousin who has been designated to translate, and the mother asks, through the cousin, whether the baptism can be in Spanish. The grandmother has come from another country for it. She does not have English and the family does not want her to stand at the font hearing words she cannot follow. It is a reasonable request in any parish and an urgent one in this one. {@pastor} does a Spanish Mass on Sundays that he learned from tapes in the nineties and reads with visible effort; he does baptisms in Spanish from the ritual with the phonetics penciled in. He is away that Sunday. The cousin explains all this to you with the neutral competence of someone who has translated for his family since he was nine. The grandmother watches your face while he talks. The ritual in Spanish is on the shelf in the sacristy. Whether you can read it as if you mean it is a question the family will answer for themselves on Sunday.
events.flavorPrompt: A language the parish needs and the priest may or may not have. The grandmother's face is the judge.

choices.label: Do it in Spanish, and do the preparation in Spanish too
choices.outcome: You send the cousin to sit with the others and talk to the mother directly. The grandmother says something about you afterward that the cousin declines to translate and the aunts laugh. On Sunday the rite is in Spanish start to finish, and the grandmother answers the renunciations in a voice that carries. Word moves through the community faster than through the bulletin: the new priest speaks. Next month there are four more.

choices.label: Read the Spanish ritual as best you can and let the family carry it
choices.outcome: You practice it three evenings with the cousin, who is patient. On Sunday you read it slowly and the family answers strongly, covering for you, which is what a family does. The grandmother thanks you with both hands. You know the difference between a rite that was said and a rite that was spoken, and so does she, and she has chosen to be grateful. You order the language course that night.

choices.label: Ask {@brother_priest} from across the diocese to come and do it
choices.outcome: He says yes, because that is what the presbyterate is for on a good day, and drives forty minutes to baptize a child he will never see again. The family is served well. You stand in the sanctuary and assist and are, correctly, a guest at your own parish's font. {@brother_priest} does not mention it, which means it counts, and you owe him one.

events.title: Same Address
events.body: The marriage file has one address on it for both of them, and neither has tried to hide it. They are thirty and thirty-one, they own the condominium together, and they have come to {parish} because her grandmother was married here and because his mother has said she will not attend a wedding on a beach. They are pleasant, serious, and braced. He says, when you have gone through the paperwork, that they have heard the priest will make them live apart until the wedding, and asks whether that is true, in the tone of a man who has already decided it is not going to happen. She adds that they have been together six years and are not going to pretend. {@pastor}'s practice is unknown to you; {@dre}, who runs the marriage preparation, says he asks and then forgets to follow up, and that the couples know it. The date they want is eleven months out. The preparation is yours to run. Nothing in the law forbids the marriage. Everything in the parish has an opinion about whether you should say anything.
events.flavorPrompt: A conversation about sin that is really a conversation about respect. The couple are not the problem and are not innocent either.

choices.label: Say what the Church teaches, once, clearly, and then get on with the preparation
choices.outcome: You say it in two sentences: what the Church holds about marriage and the body, and that you would be lying to them if you skipped it. Then you say the rest of the preparation is about the fifty years after the wedding, not the eleven months before. She looks relieved. He looks like a man who expected a fight and has been given a fact. The preparation goes well. They do not move apart and they do not lie to you about it.

choices.label: Ask them to live apart for the last months, as a preparation, and mean it
choices.outcome: You ask it as an invitation, not a condition, and you explain why: that abstinence before the vow is the vow rehearsed. He refuses on the spot. She does not, and they argue about it in your office, briefly, in a way that tells you something about the marriage. They stay. They keep the date. She confesses the week before the wedding and he does not, and the wedding is fine, and the grandmother's friends approve of the young priest who said something.

choices.label: Leave it; it is not your parish and they did not ask
choices.outcome: You run the preparation as written and it is a good preparation. They like you. {@dre} notices that you did not raise it and mentions it to {@pastor} as a compliment, which is not how he takes it. You have made two friends of the parish and been, in a small way, less than a priest to them, and you know which of the two you will remember.

events.title: Pending
events.body: The bride has a prior marriage. It lasted three years, ended nine years ago, and the petition for a declaration of nullity has been at the tribunal for fourteen months. She was told it would take twelve. Her fiancé is a convert who came into the Church for her, and his sponsor was {@parishioner}, who is now on the phone to you about it. The couple have set a date, six months out, at the hall attached to {parish}, with a deposit paid on the strength of an assurance from a priest at her previous parish that it would be fine. It is not fine. Until the decree is in hand she is not free to marry and the church cannot be booked, and every priest knows this, and every priest also knows a couple who was told otherwise. Her mother has already bought the dress. The fiancé asks you, calmly, whether there is anyone you can call. {@pastor} says the tribunal is the tribunal and hands you the file. The judicial vicar's name is on the letterhead. You have met him once, at a clergy day, for four minutes.
events.flavorPrompt: The machinery of a tribunal against a wedding calendar. The priest at the previous parish who said it would be fine is the ghost in the room.

choices.label: Tell them the truth: no date until the decree, and you will write the tribunal for a status
choices.outcome: You say it in the office with the fiancé holding her hand: the Church cannot marry her until the Church says she is free, and no priest can promise otherwise. You write the tribunal a formal request for the status of the case, copy {@pastor}, and tell the couple that the hall deposit is between them and the hall. She cries. He thanks you for being the first person to say the thing straight. The mother of the bride does not.

choices.label: Pencil the date, tell them to keep planning, and hope the decree comes
choices.outcome: You do what the priest at her previous parish did, and for the same reasons: the odds are good, the case is a straightforward one on paper, and the family is in front of you. You write it on the church calendar in pencil. {@secretary} sees the pencil and says nothing, which is worse than if she had. Five months of planning proceed on a foundation you know to be nothing. You tell yourself it is a pastoral judgment.

effects.value: Pencilled a wedding date before a decree of nullity

choices.label: Call {@chancellor} and ask, as a favor, where the case is
choices.outcome: {@chancellor} takes the call because the chancery knows your name, and that is the whole reason it works. The case is with the defender of the bond and has been for six weeks; the judge is behind by forty cases. No promise is made and none is asked for. You tell the couple the truth about the date and the truth about the queue. It is not a favor exactly. It is a debt, and both of you know it.

events.title: The Decree
events.body: The envelope from the tribunal is addressed to the petitioner in care of the parish, and {@secretary} brings it to you unopened, as she should. You call the bride and she comes within the hour with the fiancé and her mother, and she opens it in the office with her hands shaking and reads it twice. Affirmative. The sentence is in the plain, careful language the tribunal uses, with the finding on the grounds and the standard note that the decree has executive force. It is dated eleven days before the date on the church calendar. The mother of the bride sits down. The fiancé says nothing at all and then laughs. The wedding can happen, on the date, in the church, with everything the family bought. It is very nearly the thing every priest who ever pencilled a date was counting on, and it has arrived, and it does not change what you did or did not do six months ago. {@pastor} has been told the envelope came and is waiting to hear how it reads.
events.flavorPrompt: Relief that arrives on time and settles nothing about the past. The envelope, the shaking hands, the pastor waiting down the hall.

choices.label: Book the church properly now, and do the wedding with everything you have
choices.outcome: It is a good wedding. The convert weeps at the vows and his sponsor {@parishioner} is in the second pew, and the bride's mother forgives you, or forgets, which in a parish is the same thing. You preach on the long wait and the patience of God without saying the word tribunal. Nobody in the pews knows how close it came, and that is exactly as it should be.

choices.label: Tell {@pastor} you pencilled the date, before he hears it from {@secretary}
choices.outcome: He already knew. He lets you finish and then tells you, without raising his voice, what would have happened if the sentence had been negative: the family, the hall, the diocese, his name on the letter. He says the previous parish's priest is a fool and that you were his apprentice for six months. Then he says the wedding is yours, and you do it well, and you never pencil a date again.

choices.label: Write {@chancellor} a note, by hand, and copy no one
choices.outcome: Three sentences, no request, no flattery. The chancery remembers who writes and who does not, and you have learned that the diocese is run in part by handwritten notes between men who do not otherwise speak. The wedding is on the date. {@chancellor} does not reply, and mentions your name the following month in a meeting you are not in.

events.title: Mother of the Bride
events.body: The couple are twenty-four and have opinions about nothing. The bride's mother has opinions about everything: the readings, which she has chosen; the music, about which she has already spoken to {@music_director}, twice, in a tone {@music_director} has reported to you; the unity candle, which she has bought; the flowers, which will be on the altar itself; the photographer, who will need to stand in the sanctuary; and the homily, for which she has helpfully provided notes on the couple. The couple sit through the meeting like defendants. When the mother steps out to take a call, the bride says, very quickly, that they do not want any of it and cannot say so. The groom nods. The mother comes back in. She asks whether the parish has a wedding coordinator and, when told the parish has {@secretary}, says she will bring her own. {@pastor}, consulted, says weddings are yours now and that he has buried three of this woman's relatives and would like to keep it to that.
events.flavorPrompt: Light, dry, precise. The couple's silence is the real subject.

choices.label: Schedule the next meeting with the couple only, and hold to it
choices.outcome: You tell the mother, pleasantly, that the preparation sessions are for the couple and that the parish requires it, which is nearly true. She is offended for a day. In the second meeting the bride chooses the readings herself, and they are better. The wedding has the unity candle, because that fight was not worth having, and the photographer stays out of the sanctuary, because that one was. The couple thank you in a card that the mother did not write.

choices.label: Let the mother run it; it is one afternoon
choices.outcome: The unity candle, the flowers on the altar, the photographer in the sanctuary, a homily built partly from her notes. {@music_director} plays what she asked and does not speak to you for a week. The wedding is beautiful and the couple look, throughout, like guests at it. The mother tells everyone at the club that the new priest is easy to work with, which is a sentence that will follow you.

choices.label: Go through the wedding rite with the mother, item by item, and let the book say no
choices.outcome: You put the Order of Celebrating Matrimony on the desk and open it. You show her where the readings come from and why hers do not qualify, where the music is governed, where the sanctuary is described. She cannot argue with a book and does not try. She respects you for it, in the way people respect a wall. The couple get most of what they wanted without ever having to say so, and the mother's own pastor, at the reception, asks you who taught you to do that.

events.title: Friday Night, Six O'Clock
events.body: The rehearsal is at six on Friday and the best man arrives at six-twenty from something that started at two. He is loud in the vestibule, affectionate in the aisle, and by the time you have the wedding party in their places he has told the maid of honor something that has made her cry. The groom is embarrassed and protective of him in the way of men who have been friends since they were nine. The bride's father, standing at the back with his arms folded, has decided what he thinks of the whole family. The rehearsal has to happen. Tomorrow the church will hold two hundred people at two in the afternoon, and this man will carry the rings and, if the plan holds, give a toast in front of all of them. You have a rehearsal to run, a dinner to attend afterward that the couple have asked you to bless, and a decision about how much of this is your business. {@maintenance} is waiting to lock up and has seen worse, and says so.
events.flavorPrompt: Comedy shading into something sadder. Keep the best man human; keep the priest's authority small and real.

choices.label: Run the rehearsal around him, quickly, and say nothing
choices.outcome: You keep it short and keep him moving, and it is over in thirty-five minutes. He is quieter by the end. At the dinner you bless the meal and leave early. On Saturday he is grey-faced and sober and carries the rings without incident, and his toast is short because someone has spoken to him. It was not you. You are not sure it should have been.

choices.label: Walk him outside and talk to him, one man to another
choices.outcome: You take him out to the steps while the groom runs the party through the processional. He is angry for a minute and then, suddenly, not: the groom is the last friend he has, and he has been drinking since he heard the date. You listen. You do not fix it. You tell him what time to be in the sacristy tomorrow. He is there at one-fifteen, showered, and shakes your hand like it means something.

choices.label: Tell the groom, privately, that his friend does not carry the rings tomorrow in that state
choices.outcome: You say it without heat: the groom's call, but you will not have a man stumble at the altar in front of the bride's family. The groom is stung and then grateful and gives the rings to his brother. The best man finds out at the dinner and leaves. He is at the wedding, sober, in the fourth pew, and gives no toast. The bride's father approves of you completely. The groom does, less.

events.title: Under the Oak
events.body: They want to be married under the oak at her parents' place, by the water, at sunset. They have a photograph of the oak. They are both Catholic, both practicing, both in the choir, and they have done everything else right: the preparation, the paperwork, the retreat. They know it is unusual. They have read, online, that some dioceses allow it now with permission from the bishop, and that others do not, and they would like to know which kind {diocese} is and whether you would ask. {@pastor}'s answer, delivered by {@dre} in passing, was that the church is where the Church is. {@music_director}, who directs them both, has said he will bring a keyboard to the oak if it comes to that. You know the law: marriage between two Catholics is to be celebrated in a parish church, and the local ordinary may permit another suitable place. You do not know the current policy of the chancery, and asking will put your name on a question the chancery may not want asked. The bride says they will get married in church if the answer is no, and mean it, and you believe her.
events.flavorPrompt: A good couple asking an honest question of an institution that has two answers. Canon 1118. The oak is real.

choices.label: Write {@vicar_general} and ask the question properly
choices.outcome: You write a careful letter describing the couple, the place, and the reasons, and asking whether the ordinary would grant permission. The answer comes back in ten days: not in this diocese, not at present, with a paragraph on the theology of the church building that you suspect was written for someone else. The couple marry in {parish} and are gracious about it. Your name is now attached, at the chancery, to a request that was denied.

choices.label: Tell them no, and tell them why the church building matters
choices.outcome: You do not send it up. You sit with them for an hour and explain what a church is: the place where the parish gathers, where their children will be baptized, where one of them will bury the other. It is a good hour. The groom is persuaded and the bride is not, quite, but she chooses {parish} without resentment. {@music_director} is a little disappointed about the keyboard. {@pastor} hears that you handled it and did not bother the chancery, and approves.

choices.label: Tell them which neighboring diocese permits it, and let them decide
choices.outcome: You know the policy two dioceses over because you read those things, and you tell them, with the caveat that you cannot officiate there without faculties and paperwork and that {parish} loses the wedding. They think about it for a week and choose the oak, and a priest of that diocese marries them under it. {@music_director} loses two choir members for a Saturday. {@pastor} says, not to you, that the vicar gave away a wedding.

events.title: The Parking Lot
events.body: Saturday confessions, the fourth penitent, a man's voice you half recognize through the screen. He confesses, among ordinary things, that he hit a man with his car eight months ago on the county road at night and drove on, and that the man was in the paper the next day, and that he has not slept properly since. He is sorry in the way that is unmistakable. You do what a confessor does: you ask whether he is prepared to make it right, and he says he does not know, and you tell him that reparation is part of what he has come for, and you give him absolution, because contrition is not the same as courage and the sacrament is not a bargaining table. He leaves. Twenty minutes later you walk out to the parking lot and he is there, by the side door, laughing with {@pastor} about the football. He ushers the 11:00. You know his name now. You know what he did. You may never, by word or sign or in any manner, for any reason, let anyone know, including him, outside that box. He waves.
events.flavorPrompt: The seal as a physical weight. Canon 983. No melodrama; the football conversation is the horror.

choices.label: Wave back. Carry it. Say nothing, ever, to anyone
choices.outcome: You wave. You say hello at the 11:00 every week for the rest of your time at {parish}. You never look at him differently and it costs you something every Sunday to manage that. He comes back to confession twice; you do not know whether it is him until he speaks, and each time you tell him the same thing about reparation. Whether he ever goes to the sheriff you never learn. This is the priesthood, and no one told you it would feel like this.

choices.label: Take the weight, without the facts, to your own confessor
choices.outcome: You know the boundary exactly: you may speak of your own burden and never of his. You go to {@brother_priest}, who hears confessions for half the priests of {diocese}, and you tell him that you have heard something you will carry for life and that you do not know how. He says he has three of those. He says the sacrament does not ask you to be strong, only silent. You sleep. You wave at the 11:00.

choices.label: Preach on restitution the next Sunday, in general terms, and let him hear it
choices.outcome: The homily is about Zacchaeus and the fourfold repayment, and it is a good homily, and forty people hear it as meant for them because that is what homilies do. He is in the back, ushering. You do not look at him. You have not broken the seal; you have walked to its edge and looked over, and you know that this was for you and not for him, and that a confessor who preaches at his penitents is a confessor who will one day slip.

effects.value: Preached at a penitent from the pulpit

events.title: Second Grade
events.body: Forty-one second-graders, their parents in the pews, and two priests: you and {@pastor}, who has done this thirty times and looks at his watch. {@dre} has drilled them for eight weeks. They come one at a time to the chair set up by the side altar, without the screen, because {@dre} believes in the face-to-face and has told the parents so. They are terrified and thrilled in equal measure. The first one forgets the words and starts to cry. The second one confesses that he hit his sister, then that he hit his other sister, then, on reflection, that he hit the dog. The third has memorized the act of contrition in a way that has stripped it of meaning and delivers it like a spelling word. A girl, seventh or eighth in line, tells you that she has done nothing wrong and is only here because her mother made her, and looks you in the eye. Her mother is thirty feet away. {@pastor}'s line is moving twice as fast as yours. You have thirty-four to go and a rosary group at seven.
events.flavorPrompt: Warm, exact, a little funny, never cute. The girl who has done nothing wrong is the one to get right.

choices.label: Take the time each one needs, and let {@pastor} take the overflow
choices.outcome: You do not hurry. The girl who has done nothing wrong gets three minutes and, at the end of them, a real confession, quiet and hers, and a look of astonishment at what it is like to be forgiven for something specific. {@pastor} takes twenty-six and you take fifteen, and he says nothing about it, and {@dre} says a great deal, to the parents, about the young priest. You are late for the rosary and no one minds.

choices.label: Keep the line moving; it is the sacrament that matters, not the conversation
choices.outcome: Ninety seconds each, absolution, the next one. It is valid, it is complete, and it is over by six-forty. The girl who has done nothing wrong is told, kindly, that everyone has something, and absolved for whatever it is, and goes back to her mother unchanged. {@pastor} approves of your efficiency. {@dre} does not mention you to the parents at all.

choices.label: Stop the line for the girl and talk to her about what confession actually is
choices.outcome: You put the line on hold for five minutes, which {@pastor} notices, and you ask her what she thinks the sacrament is for. She thinks it is for bad children. You tell her, in words a seven-year-old can hold, that it is for people who want to be closer to God than they are, and ask if she is one of those. She thinks about it seriously and says yes. Her mother, later, tells {@dre} her daughter came home and apologized to her brother unprompted. {@dre} tells everyone.

events.title: The Line Outside
events.body: Saturday afternoon, three-thirty to four-thirty, the box, and a woman who has not been to confession in thirty-one years. She says so at the start and then begins at the beginning, and she is thorough. At the twenty-minute mark you can hear the line outside shifting; at thirty-five, someone leaves; at forty, {@secretary} knocks once on the door of the box to remind you the 5:00 Mass has a wedding party arriving for photographs beforehand. The woman is not rambling. She is doing what the sacrament invites, for the first time since she was a girl, and she is at the part of her life that is the reason she stopped coming. You can feel the shape of it approaching. If you interrupt her now she will be absolved and she will not come back. If you let her finish, six people outside will not be heard today, and one of them has been at the door every Saturday for a year and knows exactly what time you are supposed to come out.
events.flavorPrompt: The box as a pressure chamber. The line outside is real people, not an abstraction.

choices.label: Let her finish. The line will keep or it will not
choices.outcome: Sixty-eight minutes. She gets to it, and it is what you thought, and you say what the Church says about it and she has never heard it said that way. She goes out white-faced and lighter. Four people have left. Two have stayed, including the Saturday regular, who says nothing and is very brief. {@secretary} mentions the wedding photographs to {@pastor}, who mentions them to you. The woman is at the 9:00 the next morning, and the morning after that.

choices.label: Bring her gently to a close, absolve her, and ask her to come and see you Tuesday
choices.outcome: You do it as kindly as you can: you tell her she has confessed enough for the sacrament and you absolve her, and you say the rest deserves more than a box on a Saturday and give her a time. She agrees, shaken. You hear the other six. On Tuesday she does not come. You see her once more, at Christmas, at the back, and then not again. You did the reasonable thing. It was not the right one, or it was, and you will not know.

choices.label: Step out for thirty seconds and ask {@pastor} to open the other confessional
choices.outcome: You ask her to wait one moment. {@pastor} is in the rectory kitchen and comes without a word, in a stole, and opens the far box. The line divides. You go back in and she finishes, all of it, and you say what needs saying. Afterward {@pastor} says that the other box has been closed for six years because he never had a vicar who asked, and that the wedding party can take their photographs in the garden. It is the closest he has come to a compliment.

events.title: The Penance Service
events.body: The Advent penance service is the Tuesday of the third week, seven o'clock, the church half full and the parish's habit being that everyone waits for the visiting priests because the visiting priests do not know them. {@pastor} has arranged four confessors from around the deanery. Two arrive. One calls from the road to say he is coming; he does not. The fourth, {@brother_priest}, is in the sacristy vesting and tells you that the third has a problem that everyone in the deanery knows about and no one says, and that he will not be coming to any penance service this Advent. That leaves three priests for two hundred people, and the Liturgy of the Word has not started. You can hear {@music_director} playing the entrance over again. Some of the two hundred have come specifically to avoid confessing to you or to {@pastor}. A few of them will go home if the line is too long, and they will not come back until the Lenten service, if then. {@brother_priest} says: we start, and we go until we finish, and we do not talk about the third man tonight.
events.flavorPrompt: The presbyterate holding itself together on a Tuesday night. The absent priest is a shadow, not a subject.

choices.label: Three priests, go until the church is empty
choices.outcome: Two hours and twenty minutes. {@music_director} runs out of Advent hymns and starts in on chant. The last penitent leaves at a quarter to ten and {@brother_priest} shakes your hand in the sacristy and says that is how it is done. {@pastor} orders pizza for the three of you and no one mentions the third man, and the not-mentioning is a thing you have now taken part in.

choices.label: Ask {@brother_priest}, in the sacristy, what the problem is
choices.outcome: He tells you, briefly: the bottle, for three years, and a pastor's chair he should not be sitting in, and a vicar for clergy who has been told twice. It is not your business and now it is your knowledge. You hear confessions until ten with it in your head. You have entered the presbyterate's real conversation, the one about its own, and you cannot leave it now.

choices.label: Announce that confessors are short, and ask people to keep it brief
choices.outcome: You say it from the ambo, tactfully. It works: the lines move, the church is empty by nine-fifteen, and everyone who stayed was heard. But you have told two hundred people to hurry the sacrament, and one of them, a woman with a great deal to say, went home. {@pastor} thinks it was sensible. {@brother_priest} says nothing about it, and would have stayed until eleven.

events.title: Three in the Morning
events.body: The rectory phone at 3:10. A daughter's voice, controlled: her mother is dying at the county hospital, the nurse says hours, and the mother has asked for a priest, by name, and the name is {@pastor}'s. {@pastor} is asleep two doors down with the phone unplugged, which is his arrangement and which he told you about your first week. You are the priest on call, which is to say you are the priest. The oils are in the cabinet and the pyx has a host in it from the last sick call, and it is a twenty-five minute drive, thirty in the fog. You have the 6:30 Mass and a school Mass at 8:15 and a funeral at ten, and you were awake until midnight with the funeral homily. The daughter is waiting on the line. You could wake {@pastor}. You could tell the daughter that her mother has been anointed before, which she has, twice, and that you will come first thing. Or you could get dressed.
events.flavorPrompt: Fog, a pyx, a phone. The mundane logistics of a holy thing at an unholy hour.

choices.label: Go, and stay until it is over
choices.outcome: You anoint her at four and give Viaticum, and the apostolic pardon, and she knows what it is and says amen. Then you stay, because the daughter is alone, and the mother dies at ten past six with the two of you saying the rosary badly. You say the 6:30 forty minutes late to eleven people who do not complain. The funeral homily is worse than you wrote it. The daughter tells the whole parish, and the parish tells {@pastor}.

choices.label: Go, anoint her, give Viaticum, and be back for the 6:30
choices.outcome: You are there by a quarter to four and gone by half past. The sacrament is the sacrament and she receives it. The daughter thanks you at the elevator with the face of a woman who wanted you to stay and knows it is not fair to say so. You say the 6:30 on time, grey. The mother dies at seven. The daughter does not blame you, exactly.

choices.label: Wake {@pastor}; she asked for him by name
choices.outcome: You knock. He is angry for as long as it takes him to hear the name, and then he is dressed in four minutes and gone. He was her pastor for nineteen years. He comes back at seven, says the 6:30 was yours and you should have said it, and thanks you, once, in the hallway, without looking at you. She died with the priest she wanted. You slept, and are not sure you should have.

events.title: The Night Nurse
events.body: Your Thursday hospital rounds. {@parishioner} is on the fourth floor after a fall, cheerful, thin, asking after the parish, and you bring Communion and the bulletin and talk about the roof. On your way out the charge nurse stops you by the station. She is a parishioner too, at the 5:00 Saturday, and she has been a nurse for twenty-six years, and she says it flatly: he is not here for a fall. He is here because the fall was the third in a month and the scans found what they found, and the family has decided, as a family, that he is not to be told, because he is eighty-one and it would frighten him. The doctor has gone along with it so far. She has not, and cannot say so to the family, and has said so to you. He has perhaps two months. He has been asking, she says, whether he should get his affairs in order and everyone has been laughing it off. She would like a priest to do what a priest is for. Then she goes back to her station, and you are in the corridor with a pyx and a decision that is not yours and has been handed to you anyway.
events.flavorPrompt: A corridor, a nurse who has decided to speak, an old man who has been laughed at. The priest's authority here is moral, not medical.

choices.label: Go back in, sit down, and ask him what he wants to know
choices.outcome: You do not tell him. You ask. It takes him a minute to understand that you are asking for real, and then he says: is it bad. You say you think he should ask his doctor to tell him everything, and that you will be there when he does. He does. The family is furious with the doctor, then with you, then, when he makes his confession and settles his will and calls his brother in another state, not. He dies in seven weeks, prepared.

choices.label: Call the family that evening and tell them what you think a dying man is owed
choices.outcome: The eldest daughter takes the call. She is defensive and then, when you say that her father has been asking whether to get his affairs in order, silent. You say the Church does not require him to know, but that you have never seen a man die well who was lied to. She talks to her siblings. Two days later they tell him together, with you in the room. It is terrible and right. The nurse nods at you in the corridor the following Thursday.

choices.label: Anoint him next week on a pretext, and leave the family's decision to the family
choices.outcome: You come back on Tuesday and say that the parish anoints everyone over eighty in hospital now, which is very nearly true, and he receives it gladly. He does not make a confession because he does not know he is dying. He dies at home in six weeks, surprised, and the family are grateful to you for the anointing and never know what the nurse told you. She knows. She moves to the 9:00 Sunday, where {@pastor} presides.

events.title: The Same Three Points
events.body: A man at the 10:30 stops you at the door. He is polite. He is a lector, an accountant, a man who listens. He says, not unkindly, that he enjoyed the homily and that he enjoyed it the first time too, in October, when the Gospel was different and the three points were the same, and that his wife had wondered at the time whether the three points were going to be the three points from the diaconate homily he had heard at his nephew's parish. He says the parish knows you are stretched. He says it as a friend. Then he goes to brunch. You stand at the door shaking hands and doing arithmetic. Four Masses this weekend, a funeral, a wedding, the hospital, and a Wednesday night with the confirmation class, and the homily got an hour on Saturday afternoon and the hour was mostly finding the old file. {@pastor} preaches the same eight homilies on a rotation and has for thirty years, and no one stops him at the door, because he is the pastor and because he stopped pretending they were new sometime in the last century.
events.flavorPrompt: Small, deflating, exact. The accountant is right and kind, which is the worst combination. The recycled homily is the corrosive habit of DESIGN 2.6.

choices.label: Write every homily fresh from now on and find the hours somewhere
choices.outcome: You find them in sleep and in the visits you used to make on Thursday afternoons. The homilies improve, slowly; the accountant nods at you at the door in a way that means he has noticed. Two Thursdays a month the fourth floor at the hospital does not see you. Nobody stops you at the door about that, because the people on the fourth floor are not at the door.

choices.label: Tell him he is right, thank him, and change nothing this month
choices.outcome: You say it plainly: you are stretched, it was the October homily with a new introduction, and you are grateful he told you instead of his wife telling the parish. He respects that. It buys you the month. The month goes as the last one went, and in the spring it is a different man at the door, less polite. The habit is now a habit.

choices.label: Ask {@pastor} to take one of your weekend Masses so you can preach properly at the others
choices.outcome: He looks at you for a while and says that when he was a vicar he preached six a weekend and wrote every one, which is not true, and then he takes the Saturday 5:00. Three homilies a weekend, all new. The accountant notices by Advent. {@pastor} mentions at the deanery meeting that his vicar asked for a lighter load, and the deanery hears what it wants to hear.

events.title: Could You Send Me the Text
events.body: It was a good homily. You knew it at the ambo, which is rare and dangerous, and the church knew it too: the particular stillness, the woman in the third pew who stopped fanning herself, the two men at the back who did not leave after Communion. The Gospel was the rich young man and you said something true about wanting to be told what to do and not wanting to do it, and it landed on a parish that has money and knows it. At the door, a parishioner who edits the diocesan paper asks whether you have it written out and whether she could run it. On Tuesday a man from the parish who does something on the radio asks the same. On Wednesday {@pastor}, who preached the 9:00 on the same Gospel to the usual attention, says at dinner that he heard it went well, and asks what you said, and listens to your summary with his eyes on his plate. {@music_director} says it is the first time in four years anyone has talked about a homily in the choir loft. There is a version of this week where nothing happens, and it is closing.
events.flavorPrompt: The cost of high Charisma: envy at the dinner table. Keep the homily's content vague and the parish's reaction specific.

choices.label: Send the editor the text and let it run
choices.outcome: It runs on page five with your name and {parish}. The chancery reads the diocesan paper, and {@bishop}'s secretary clips it. Three priests write to say it was good, and one of them means it. {@pastor} does not mention it, and at the next deanery meeting refers to you, once, as our columnist. You are now a man who has been in print, which is a thing the diocese does not forget in either direction.

choices.label: Decline, gracefully; a homily is for the people who were there
choices.outcome: You tell her a homily is spoken to a church, not written for a paper, and that you would rather it stayed at {parish}. She is disappointed and thinks better of you. {@pastor}, hearing you turned it down, says nothing, and passes you the salt, and something at the table relaxes. The radio man stops asking. The homily is remembered for a few months by the people who heard it and then it is gone, like all of them.

choices.label: Ask the editor to run it under {parish}'s name with no byline, and tell {@pastor} first
choices.outcome: You take it to him before you answer her. You say the parish could use the notice and that you would rather it not be about you. He looks at you as if trying to find the angle, and there is none, and he says all right. It runs as from the parish. The chancery knows anyway, because the chancery always knows, and files you under a heading that will do you good later. {@pastor} is, for a month, easy to live with.

events.title: Apostle to the Apostles
events.body: The feast of St. Mary Magdalene falls on a Sunday this year, or near enough that you preach her at the weekday Mass with the school in attendance, and you say what the Church has said since the feast was raised: that she was the first to see the risen Lord and the first sent to tell of it, apostle to the apostles, and you say something, in passing, about women and the Church that you thought was uncontroversial. By Tuesday {@secretary} has three messages. One is from a mother who says her daughter came home asking why women cannot be priests and wants to know what you told the children. One is from a parishioner who is a lawyer and wants a copy of what you said, exactly. One is from a man who says he has been waiting thirty years for a priest to say it and would like to shake your hand. {@pastor} has had a fourth call, from someone on the finance council, and passes it on to you without comment, which is comment. {@dre} says it was a good homily and that you should not have given it to second-graders. You have a parish that has decided, in two days, that you are a certain kind of priest, and it does not agree on which.
events.flavorPrompt: A homily that said less than it was heard to say. The parish sorts itself in forty-eight hours. Women_roles at semi-public volume.

choices.label: Return the calls, say exactly what you said, and stand by it
choices.outcome: You call all three. To the mother you say what the Church teaches and that her daughter's question is a good one. To the lawyer you say there is no text and summarize it honestly. To the man who waited thirty years you say thank you and nothing else. The parish's sorting hardens. The finance council man tells {@pastor} the vicar has an agenda. The man who waited thirty years is at every Mass you say for the rest of the year.

choices.label: Clarify it next Sunday, carefully, with the Catechism in hand
choices.outcome: You preach it again, properly: what the Church teaches about ordination and why, what it teaches about the dignity of women and why, and the difference between the two questions, which the second grade had collapsed. It is a good homily and it satisfies no one who was already angry. The lawyer takes notes. The mother is reassured. The man who waited thirty years looks at you afterward as if you had taken something back, and you had.

choices.label: Return no calls, preach the readings next Sunday, and let the week bury it
choices.outcome: You do nothing, which is a policy. {@secretary} tells callers that Father is at the hospital. By the second week there is a new thing to talk about. But the mother has moved her daughter's religious education to another parish, the lawyer has written it down anyway, and the man who waited thirty years does not ask to shake your hand again. {@pastor} notes that you can take a hint. It is not the compliment it sounds like.

events.title: A Priest Who Was Here
events.body: He asks for an appointment, not confession, and he is specific about the difference. He is in his late thirties, a parishioner's brother, back in town for his mother's illness, and he has not been inside a Catholic church in twenty years. He sits in the office with his coat on. He tells you that when he was thirteen there was a priest at {parish}, a vicar like you, who ran the altar servers, and he tells you what that priest did, over two years, in the sacristy and on the trips to the shrine. He tells it flatly. He has never told anyone but a therapist. The priest's name is one you know: retired now, in residence at a parish across {diocese}, still saying a Sunday Mass. {@pastor} was ordained the same year as him. He wanted, he says, to say it in the building where it happened, to someone in a collar, and see what the collar did. You know what the Charter requires. You know what {diocese} has, and has not, done with such things before. You know that the moment you pick up a phone, this stops being a conversation and becomes a process, and that the process is the right thing, and that he may feel handed off.
events.flavorPrompt: Sensitive: authored only, never skinned. The man's account is not narrated in detail. The institution's machinery is the subject. Reporting up is correct and it costs.

choices.label: Tell him what you are required to do, and call the victim assistance coordinator and {@vicar_for_clergy} today
choices.outcome: You tell him first: that you believe him, that you are obliged to report this to the diocese and to civil authorities, and that a person whose job is to help him will call within a day. He is angry that it has become a form. You make both calls before he has left the parking lot. By evening {@vicar_for_clergy} has the retired priest's faculties suspended pending review. By the weekend {@pastor} knows whose classmate you have named, and looks at you as if you had done it to him.

choices.label: Take it to {@pastor} first and let him decide how the parish reports it
choices.outcome: {@pastor} listens with his hands flat on the desk. He says he will handle it. He says the man is a classmate and that he will call him, and then the chancery. Ten days later nothing has been called. You ask, and he says these things take care, and you realize that the report is now yours to make over his head or not at all, and that ten days have passed with a man across {diocese} still saying a Sunday Mass. The parishioner's brother has not called back.

choices.label: Report it today, and tell him you will go with him to every meeting if he wants you there
choices.outcome: You make the calls with him in the room, on speaker, so that he hears the words used about him. Then you say you will be at the review board interview, the meeting with the coordinator, the conversation with the police, whichever he wants. He takes you up on two of the three. It costs you a day a week for a month and {@pastor} the best part of his friendship, and the man goes to his mother's funeral Mass, at {parish}, in the front pew.

events.title: The Statement
events.body: The letter from {@bishop} comes in a chancery envelope with a second, sealed one inside it. The review board has met. The allegation has been found credible. The retired priest has been permanently removed from public ministry, his name will be added to the list {diocese} publishes, and the parishes where he served, {parish} first among them, will be told at every Mass this weekend by the reading of a statement, which is the sealed page. {@vicar_for_clergy} calls to say the statement is to be read as written, that a victim assistance number is to be printed in the bulletin, and that the bishop is grateful for the way the matter was brought forward, in a tone that does not say whether that is a compliment. {@pastor} has been sent the same letter. He has said, through {@secretary}, that he will read it at the 9:00 and that you will read it at the others. The parish does not yet know. By Sunday evening it will, and it will also know, because parishes know, which priest made the call. The man who sat in your office with his coat on has been told the outcome by the coordinator and has not called you.
events.flavorPrompt: Sensitive: authored only. The bureaucracy doing the right thing, slowly and at a cost. The sealed page is the object.

choices.label: Read the statement as written, at every Mass, and add nothing
choices.outcome: You read it in a level voice at three Masses. The church is silent in a way it is not silent for anything else. An old man walks out at the 5:00. A woman at the 11:00 waits for you afterward and says the retired priest baptized her children, and that she does not know what to do with that, and you say neither do you. The chancery notes that {parish} handled it without incident. {@pastor}'s 9:00 statement, you hear, was read very quickly.

choices.label: Read it, and then say, in your own words, that the parish should have been told twenty years ago
choices.outcome: Three sentences after the statement, unscripted, about the years of silence and the people who lived inside it. At the 11:00 there is applause, which you did not want. By Monday {@vicar_for_clergy} has called {@pastor} to ask what the vicar added, and by Wednesday the local paper has a paragraph with your name in it. The man who sat in your office sends a card, unsigned, with the date of the Mass on it. The chancery's gratitude has a new tone.

choices.label: Make the call you should have made ten days in, and tell {@vicar_for_clergy} the truth about the delay
choices.outcome: You tell {@vicar_for_clergy} the date the man came to you and the date you are calling, and whose desk it sat on between. He does not thank you. The process runs from that day, and the statement you read on Sunday is the same statement it would have been, and the retired priest said two more Sunday Masses than he should have. {@pastor} does not speak to you for a month. The chancery file has your name in it now, on both sides of the page.

choices.label: Ask {@pastor} to read it at every Mass himself; it was his classmate and his parish
choices.outcome: He refuses, and then he does it, all five Masses, in a voice the parish has not heard from him, and it is the right thing and you made him do it. The parish blames him for the news and you for the silence, which is unfair to both of you. {@vicar_for_clergy} hears that the vicar did not read the statement and draws a conclusion you will not be able to correct.

events.title: Would You Just Talk to Him
events.body: {@parishioner} catches you after the 9:00 and asks a favor, in the voice people use for favors they have rehearsed. Her brother. He is fifty-one, he lives four streets from the church, he was an altar boy here and has not been to Mass since their father's funeral in the last century, and he is, she says, not angry at the Church, just done with it. He is coming to her house for dinner on Thursday. Would you come. She has not told him you are coming. She says he will be polite because he is always polite, and that if anyone can reach him it is a priest who is not the priest who buried their father, about whom there is a story she does not tell you. You have a wake on Thursday at seven, which you could move. You have also been the subject of this kind of dinner yourself, in one form or another, and you remember how it felt from the other chair. She is waiting with her car keys in her hand.
events.flavorPrompt: A sister's ambush dinner. The brother is not a project; the priest knows it and goes anyway, or not.

choices.label: Go, and talk about anything but the Church unless he raises it
choices.outcome: You go. He is polite, and then, when he sees that you are not going to do what he expected, curious. You talk about the neighborhood, the old school, a coach you both turn out to have hated. He raises it himself over coffee, one question, about the priest who buried his father, and you answer honestly that you do not know the man. He does not come to Mass. He waves to you on the street, which in that neighborhood is a start.

choices.label: Tell her no, kindly, and that she should tell him you would be glad to see him if he ever asks
choices.outcome: You say you will not walk into a man's sister's kitchen uninvited by him, and that you have been on the other side of that table. She is disappointed and thinks you are being difficult. Eight months later he comes to the rectory on his own, on a weekday, and says his sister told him what you said, and that it was the first thing a priest had said that he agreed with. It takes a year after that.

choices.label: Go, and over dessert ask him straight out what happened at his father's funeral
choices.outcome: You ask. The table goes still. He tells it: a priest who mispronounced the name, twice, and left before the burial, and a family that had given the parish forty years. It is a small story and it has held him for thirty years. You say the priest was wrong. He looks at his sister, who has never heard you say a priest was wrong, and something moves. He does not come back to Mass. He comes to the parish picnic, which is not nothing.

events.title: The Tuesday Class
events.body: The OCIA class, which everyone in {parish} still calls RCIA, meets Tuesdays in the hall with {@dre} and, this year, with you, because {@pastor} has decided the vicar should teach the sacraments unit. Eleven adults: four catechumens, seven candidates, a retired engineer who takes notes, a young woman who came because of a boyfriend and has stayed past the boyfriend. It is the week on the Eucharist, and it goes well until the engineer asks, without hostility, why he should join an institution that spent thirty years moving abusers from parish to parish, and whether the Eucharist is supposed to make that all right. {@dre} looks at you. The young woman looks at her hands. Nobody in the room has asked the question out loud before, and everybody in the room has asked it. You have a good answer about the holiness of the Church and the sinfulness of its members, and you know it is a good answer, and you know it is the answer he has already read and found wanting. The class is watching to see whether you will give it to him anyway.
events.flavorPrompt: A real question in a church hall. The good answer and the true answer are not the same answer. No apologetics victory.

choices.label: Give him the distinction properly: the holiness of the Church, the sin of her members, the Eucharist as the one thing that was never theirs to ruin
choices.outcome: You give it, and you give it well, with Augustine on the Donatists and the fact that the sacrament does not depend on the minister, and it is true, and it is the answer he has read. He nods and writes it down. The young woman does not look up. {@dre} says afterward that it was a fine answer and that she is not sure it was for him. Two of the eleven do not come back the next week; you do not know whether that is why.

choices.label: Tell him you ask the same question and have not stopped, and that you are still here
choices.outcome: You say it: that you were ordained into this and that you have no answer that makes the thirty years all right, and that you stayed because the Eucharist is not the Church's to give or withhold, only to hand on, and that you have decided to be one of the hands. It is not an argument. The engineer stops writing. The young woman looks up. {@dre} says nothing on the way out and puts a hand on your arm. All eleven are there the next Tuesday.

choices.label: Tell him it deserves a whole evening and schedule it, and then give him the evening
choices.outcome: You say it is the right question and the wrong night, and you put it on the calendar, and {@dre} rebuilds the syllabus around it. The evening comes. You bring the Charter, the diocesan audit, the list, and the theology, and you let them argue with all of it. The engineer stays in the program and becomes, eventually, a lector who reads the hard passages well. The young woman does not come to the evening, and does not come back.

events.title: Fifteen
events.body: Saturdays at {parish} belong to the quinceañeras. There are three this Saturday, at eleven, one, and three, with a wedding at five, and {@secretary}'s book for next year is already full through August. The family for the one o'clock arrives for the preparation meeting with the girl, her parents, her madrina, and a court of fourteen teenagers who will process. The mother would like the Mass, not the blessing; a Mass, with the court in the sanctuary, the presentation of the crown and the last doll, the medal, the Bible, and the mariachi, who have been paid. The girl has not been to Mass since her First Communion and says so when asked, honestly, with her mother's hand tightening on her arm. {@pastor}'s rule is written on a card taped inside the sacristy door: Mass only if the girl is in religious education, otherwise the blessing outside Mass; no mariachi in the sanctuary; the court sits in the pews. {@pastor} does not enforce the card. {@music_director} has strong feelings about the mariachi that he has shared with you in writing. The mother is looking at you, and then at the card, and then at you.
events.flavorPrompt: A rite the parish loves and the priest may not understand. The card on the sacristy door is the pastor's absent authority.

choices.label: Enforce the card: the blessing, not the Mass, and the court in the pews
choices.outcome: You say it in your best register and it is received as what it is: a rule no one has enforced in years, enforced on this family. The mother goes to {@pastor} on Monday and he tells her the vicar is right and does the Mass himself the following month for a different family, with mariachi. You have learned the rule at {parish} is the pastor's memory of the rule. {@music_director} sends flowers.

choices.label: Do the Mass, in Spanish, and use the preparation to catechize the girl properly
choices.outcome: You meet the girl twice, alone with her madrina, and talk about what she is actually promising in front of her family, and she surprises you by listening. The Mass is in Spanish with the court in the front pews and the mariachi in the choir loft, which {@music_director} tolerates because you asked. The mother tells everyone. Next month's Saturdays are worse, because the families now ask for you by name.

choices.label: Offer the blessing outside Mass, but make it beautiful, with the court and the mariachi and the whole rite
choices.outcome: You use the approved order for the blessing on the fifteenth birthday and give it everything: the presentation of the gifts, the renewal of baptismal promises, a homily to the girl in front of her court, the mariachi at the end. It is forty minutes. The mother wanted the Mass and gets something she did not know existed, and is, after a day, pleased. {@pastor} hears it went well and says the card was always meant to be applied with judgment.

events.title: The Eight O'Clock
events.body: The eight o'clock is in English and there are ninety people at it, most of them over seventy, most of them with a parent or grandparent buried from this church when the parish was theirs. They built the school. They founded the Altar Society, which still meets, with nine members. The 10:00, 11:30, and 1:00 are in Spanish and fill the building to the doors. {@pastor} has decided, with the finance council, to move the eight o'clock to seven-thirty to make room for a fourth Spanish Mass, and has asked you to tell the Altar Society, because they like you, which is to say because he does not want to. The president of the society, a widow who has been at the eight o'clock since before you were born, receives the news in the parish kitchen and says nothing for a long moment. Then she says that they have given this parish everything they had, and that they knew this was coming, and that she would like to know whether the young priest thinks they should just go quietly. She is not asking rhetorically. The nine of them are looking at you.
events.flavorPrompt: A founding generation being scheduled out of its own church. Neither side is wrong. The kitchen and the nine women are the scene.

choices.label: Tell them the truth: the parish is theirs and it has changed, and you will be at the seven-thirty every week
choices.outcome: You do not soften it. You say the parish belongs to whoever comes, and that they came for sixty years and others are coming now, and that you will say the seven-thirty yourself and it will be as good a Mass as you can make it. The president says that is an honest answer. Seventy of the ninety come to the seven-thirty. The Altar Society sends you a card at Christmas signed by all nine.

choices.label: Go back to {@pastor} and argue that the eight o'clock stays where it is
