choices.outcome: You make the case in his office: that the ninety are the parish's memory and its only endowment, and that a fourth Spanish Mass could go at five on Saturday instead. He listens, which is more than you expected, and keeps the eight o'clock for one more year. The Altar Society regards you as their priest. The Spanish community's leaders notice who argued for whom, and file it.

choices.label: Propose that the Altar Society and the Guadalupanas run the parish festival together, and chair the first meeting
choices.outcome: The first meeting is in the hall with a translator and it is terrible, and the second is less terrible, and by the festival the president of the Altar Society and the president of the Guadalupanas have discovered they were both born in the same month of the same year and have been arguing happily ever since. The seven-thirty happens anyway. It matters less. You have spent every Tuesday evening for two months on it.

events.title: The Families in the Back
events.body: There are perhaps forty of them, and they sit in the back six pews at the 11:00, and they have been doing it for three years. They work at the plant and the nursery and the two restaurants on the highway, and they drive forty minutes to the nearest Spanish Mass on the Sundays they can, and come here on the Sundays they cannot. Their children are in the school on tuition assistance that {@dre} arranges quietly. Nobody on the parish council has mentioned them. {@parishioner}, who is on the council, mentions them to you after Mass in a tone that is not unkind and not kind either: are they going to want a Spanish Mass, and does {parish} really have the priests for that, and would it change the parish. Then a father from the back six pews stops you at the door with his daughter translating and asks, with great care, whether there could be confessions in Spanish, sometime, for the older people. Not a Mass. Just confessions. He has been building up to asking for a year.
events.flavorPrompt: The reverse of the usual story: a small Latino community in an Anglo parish, asking for the smallest thing. The council member is not a villain.

choices.label: Say yes to the confessions, in Spanish, first Saturday of the month, and tell no one who does not need to know
choices.outcome: The first Saturday, eleven people. The second, thirty, some from two counties over. {@secretary} adds a line to the bulletin without asking you. {@parishioner} sees the line and says nothing, which is a decision. By spring the back six pews are the back nine, and the father who asked brings you tamales at Christmas and does not know how to say what he means, and does not have to.

choices.label: Arrange for {@brother_priest} to come once a month for Spanish confessions, and take it to the council openly
choices.outcome: You ask {@brother_priest}, who speaks it, and he agrees for the price of a return favor. Then you put it on the council agenda, because hiding it would be worse. The council discusses it for forty minutes. {@parishioner} votes for it in the end, saying it is only confessions. It is only confessions. Everyone at the table knows it is not only confessions, and it passes anyway.

choices.label: Give the father the Mass times at the Spanish parish forty minutes away, and leave it there
choices.outcome: You say you cannot do it yourself and that the parish forty minutes away does it well, and he thanks you and takes the card. It is true and it is a refusal. {@parishioner} is relieved. The back six pews are five by summer, and four by the following year, and the father does not stop you at the door again, and you notice, every Sunday, that he does not.

events.title: The Parking Lot Is Watched
events.body: The 1:00 had three hundred people at Easter and has a hundred and twenty now, and {@dre} tells you why, because no one else will say it to the clergy: a van has been parked across the street from the lot on two Sundays, and a man from the 1:00 was taken from his driveway on a Tuesday, and the community has decided that the church is a place where you can be found. The families have not stopped believing. They have stopped coming. {@pastor} has said, at the staff meeting, that the parish does not do politics and that the bishop has not said anything, both of which are true. Then {@parishioner}, who runs the food pantry, comes to you with a request from a group of mothers: would the priests say something. Not a march. Not a statement. Just something, from the ambo, in Spanish, so that the families know the Church has noticed. There is a Sunday coming. What is said at it will be repeated in every kitchen in the parish, and, if the wrong person is in the pews, in an office downtown. What is not said will be repeated too.
events.flavorPrompt: Fear as an attendance number. The homily as a decision with consequences in two directions. Immigration at semi-public and public volume.

choices.label: Preach it at the 1:00, in Spanish, plainly: the Church's teaching on the stranger and this parish's door
choices.outcome: You say what the Church says and what the parish is: that the stranger is to be welcomed, that {parish} is a house of God and not of any government, that the families are known here by name and will be. It is not a political homily and it will be called one. A hundred and twenty people are very quiet. Ninety more are there the next week. A letter goes to {@bishop} from someone at the 9:00. {@pastor} says you did not clear it, and you did not.

choices.label: Say nothing from the ambo; host a know-your-rights evening in the hall with the diocesan Catholic Charities lawyer
choices.outcome: You do not preach. You call the diocesan office, which has a lawyer for exactly this and is glad to be asked, and the hall is full on a Thursday with people who have not been in the building in months. {@pastor} cannot object to Catholic Charities. The mothers wanted a word from the ambo and got a pamphlet and a lawyer, and understand, roughly, why. Attendance comes back slowly. The van stays.

choices.label: Add a petition at every Mass for families living in fear, and leave it at that
choices.outcome: The petition is read at all five Masses, in both languages, and it is true and it commits no one. {@pastor} approves. The mothers hear it and know exactly what it is: the most the priests were willing to say. The 1:00 stays at a hundred and twenty. {@parishioner} keeps running the pantry and does not bring you another request. You did not do the wrong thing. You have learned what that feels like.

events.title: No Room at the Inn
events.body: The school Christmas pageant is the second Thursday of Advent, in the church, because the gym is too small and because it has always been in the church, and the principal has asked you to give the blessing at the end and, if you would, to be the voice of the innkeeper, since the eighth-grader who was to do it has been suspended. The pageant is a problem in the way pageants are: the third grade has been given a song with a verse about Santa; the kindergarten angels will be in the sanctuary; the Holy Family will be played by the children of the two families on the school board who are not speaking; and {@music_director}, who was not consulted, has heard that there will be a recorded track and has written to {@pastor}, who has forwarded it to you, because the school is yours now. Four hundred parents will come, most of them not parishioners. The tuition families are the school's whole finances. The principal has been kind to you since you arrived and is a little desperate. The innkeeper has four lines.
events.flavorPrompt: Light, affectionate, precise about the small institutional frictions. The innkeeper's four lines are the priest's whole role.

choices.label: Say the four lines, give the blessing, and let the principal have her pageant
choices.outcome: You are a convincing innkeeper. The angels are in the sanctuary and nobody is struck down. The Santa verse is sung and {@music_director} sits through it with a face. Four hundred parents see a priest in a bathrobe with a towel on his head and think better of the school, and eleven of them ask about Mass times afterward. {@pastor} says the innkeeper was the best thing in it, which is not saying much, and is saying something.

choices.label: Sit down with the principal and {@music_director} together and fix the music, and then be the innkeeper
choices.outcome: One meeting, forty minutes, and the recorded track becomes {@music_director} at the piano, the Santa verse becomes a carol, and the principal gets to keep everything else. {@music_director} is so pleased to have been asked that he writes a descant for the angels. It costs you an afternoon in the last week of Advent, which you did not have. The pageant is better than anyone expected. Nobody but you knows why.

choices.label: Tell the principal the sanctuary is not a stage, and move the pageant to the gym
choices.outcome: You say it gently and it lands hard. The principal moves it, because she has no choice, and the gym holds two hundred and fifty of the four hundred, and a hundred and fifty parents stand in the hallway and remember it. {@music_director} is grateful and says so to {@pastor}. The tuition families are not, and the principal is polite to you at every subsequent function in a way that is worse than rudeness.

events.title: The Triduum Schedule
events.body: {@pastor} puts the schedule on the kitchen table on Palm Sunday night. The Chrism Mass at the cathedral Tuesday morning, both of you, an hour each way. Confessions Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday evenings, two priests, a line out the door. Tenebrae Wednesday. The Mass of the Lord's Supper Thursday with the washing of feet and the procession to the altar of repose and adoration until midnight, which someone must close. Good Friday: the Passion at three, the Spanish Via Crucis through the neighborhood at noon with a thousand people, and the Stations at seven, and the hospital, which has four parishioners dying and has asked. Holy Saturday morning, the blessing of the baskets, then the Vigil at eight-thirty with six to be baptized and the Exsultet, which is yours. Easter Sunday: five Masses. Somewhere in the week there is a funeral, because there is always a funeral, and it is Thursday morning. {@pastor} says he has done this for thirty years and it cannot all be done, and that the trick is to decide, on Palm Sunday, what will be done badly. He pushes the paper across the table.
events.flavorPrompt: Holy Week as a triage problem. Concrete, exhausted, without complaint. Something is neglected and the player chooses what.

choices.label: Do the liturgies fully and send the hospital to Easter Monday
choices.outcome: The Triduum is done as the book asks, every hour of it, and the Exsultet goes well, and the six are baptized, and the church at the Vigil is a thing you will remember. On Easter Monday you go to the hospital and one of the four has died, on Good Friday, without a priest, and the family was told Father would come. Her son is at the 9:00 the following Sunday and does not receive Communion from you. He is right.

choices.label: Cut the Wednesday confessions and Tenebrae, and go to the hospital instead
choices.outcome: You anoint all four on Wednesday, and one of them dies on Holy Saturday, prepared, and her family is at the Vigil. The Wednesday line at the confessional is turned away with a sign, and thirty people who had built up to it go to Easter unconfessed, and a few of them will not try again until Advent. Tenebrae is cancelled and the twelve people who love it write to {@pastor}. You did the corporal work and neglected the spiritual one. That is a choice with a name.

choices.label: Call every priest you know and beg for confessors, a hospital visit, and a Good Friday Stations
choices.outcome: {@brother_priest} takes Wednesday confessions. A retired priest from across {diocese} takes the hospital Thursday. A classmate drives in for the seven o'clock Stations. It all gets done, by six men, and you spend Holy Week on the phone as much as in the sanctuary, and the Exsultet is sung by a man who has slept eleven hours in four days. Every one of those priests will call you next year. That is the deal.

choices.label: Do all of it. Sleep is for Easter Monday
choices.outcome: You do all of it. Every liturgy, every confession, the hospital at six in the morning on Friday, the Via Crucis, the funeral, the Vigil, the five Masses. It is, on paper, a triumph. On Easter Sunday afternoon you fall asleep at the rectory table and {@pastor} covers you with his coat. You are ill for a week after, and the week after that you find the breviary has not been opened since Tuesday, and you do not remember deciding that.

events.title: The Exsultet
events.body: The Vigil is at eight-thirty and it is your Exsultet. {@pastor} gave it to you in February, saying his voice was not what it was and that a parish ought to hear a young man sing it, and you have practiced it in the empty church at seven in the morning for six weeks, and {@music_director} has heard you and said it was fine, which from him is a good review. At six o'clock {@dre} finds you in the sacristy with a problem: one of the six elect, a man of forty who has been in the program since September, has told her in the parking lot that he is not sure, that he wants to be baptized tonight and is not sure, and she does not know whether that is nerves or the truth and neither does he, and the fire is being built outside. The other five are vesting in white in the hall. His sponsor is {@parishioner}, who is looking for you. The Exsultet is in your head, every note. There is a man outside who is about to promise the whole of it and does not know if he means it, and two and a half hours in which to find out.
events.flavorPrompt: The most beautiful night of the year with one unresolved man in it. The fire, the dark church, the sacristy. Keep the Exsultet real.

choices.label: Go out to the parking lot and talk to him until one of you knows
choices.outcome: Forty minutes on the curb by the fire pit. He is not unsure about God. He is unsure about being someone new in front of his family, who are inside and did not want him to do this. You say that is not a reason to wait and not a reason to go ahead either, and that it is his. He goes ahead. The Exsultet is a little rough at the end; you were thinking about him. He is baptized in front of his family.

choices.label: Tell him he may wait for Pentecost, and that waiting is not failing
choices.outcome: You say it clearly: the sacrament is not a deadline and the Church has always baptized when the person is ready, and Pentecost is seven weeks away. He is relieved and ashamed and relieved. Five are baptized. The Exsultet is the best you will ever sing it. He is baptized at Pentecost with eleven people present, and it is, he tells you, exactly right, and {@dre} is not sure you did not simply solve your own problem.

choices.label: Ask {@pastor} to talk to him; you have the Exsultet to protect
choices.outcome: {@pastor} goes out to the parking lot and comes back in twelve minutes and says the man is fine, and the man is baptized, and the Exsultet is clean and strong and the church is dark and gold and you will remember it. Three weeks later the man stops coming to Mass. {@dre} does not say it is because of the twelve minutes. She does not have to.

events.title: Twice a Year
events.body: The four o'clock on Christmas Eve is yours, and it is the one with the children's pageant and the people who come twice a year, and {@maintenance} has opened the hall with a video feed for the overflow, and the overflow is overflowing. Fourteen hundred people in a church that seats nine hundred. The fire marshal is a parishioner and has gone to the 6:30 on purpose. You have never preached to this many people who do not want to be preached to. {@pastor}, who has the midnight and the 10:00 in the morning, said at lunch that the four o'clock homily is the most important seven minutes of the parish's year and that most priests waste it, either by scolding the ones who do not come or by pretending they are not there. He did not say what he would do instead. The pageant ends. The Gospel is read. Fourteen hundred faces, half of them politely absent, look up at you, and you have seven minutes and no second chance until Easter, when most of them will be back, and will be looking to see if you noticed them then.
events.flavorPrompt: The Christmas crowd as an audience the priest gets once. No scolding, no pretending. The seven minutes are the whole event.

choices.label: Preach the Incarnation, plainly, as if everyone there had come for it
choices.outcome: You say what the night is about and you say it to the back of the hall, and you do not say the word attendance. It is seven minutes. Some of them hear it. A man in a good coat stops you afterward and says he has not heard a priest talk like that in twenty years, and asks what time Mass is on an ordinary Sunday, and you tell him. He does not come. Someone else does. That is how the four o'clock works.

choices.label: Preach the manger as a place for the poor, and mean this parish's poor, by name of street
choices.outcome: You name the streets. The shelter three blocks away, the families in the motel by the highway, the pantry line on Wednesdays. You say the child was born among them and that the parish has a door on that side too. It is a good homily and it makes a certain kind of parishioner uncomfortable on the one night he came. The pantry's collection the following Wednesday is the largest in its history. A letter arrives for {@pastor} about politics from the pulpit.

choices.label: Say, warmly and directly, that the parish wants them back in January and will not ask where they have been
choices.outcome: You say it as an invitation and it is heard, by some, as a reproach, because some people can hear nothing else. Twenty new faces at the 11:00 in January, which is twenty more than last year, and a note in the collection basket that says the priest should not have made people feel bad on Christmas. {@pastor} reads the note and says every year there is one, and that you got the good version.

events.title: Fridays in Lent
events.body: The Knights run the Lenten fish fry in the hall every Friday, and they have run it since before the hall had a kitchen, and it makes the parish eleven thousand dollars a season, which is not nothing. This year there is a problem. The Grand Knight, who is {@parishioner}, has decided the beer license is a moral question and has cancelled it, and half the Knights have said they will not work the fryers without it, and the other half have said good, and the first Friday is in nine days. {@pastor} has said, to you, that he would rather the parish lost the beer than the Knights, and would rather lose neither, and that this is a good first thing for a vicar to handle. {@maintenance}, who does the setup, has said that without beer the crowd will be half, and without the crowd the Knights will not come, and without the Knights there is no fry. The parish poor box, which the fry funds, is at its lowest in six years. You have nine days and no authority, and {@parishioner} has asked you to come to the council meeting and say something.
events.flavorPrompt: A parish institution eating itself over a beer license. Dry, affectionate, procedural. The poor box is the stake.

choices.label: Beer in the hall, none in the kitchen, and the poor box gets the bar take
choices.outcome: You say it at the council meeting and it works because it gives everyone a thing to have won. The Grand Knight has the kitchen dry. The fryers have their crowd. The poor box gets the bar money, which is announced, and which makes the beer a good work. The first Friday does three hundred and forty dinners. {@pastor} says that was politics and that you should not get good at it.

choices.label: Back {@parishioner}: a Lenten fish fry does not need a bar
choices.outcome: You say it at the council, and the Grand Knight's half applaud, and the other half work the first Friday with expressions. The crowd is smaller. The take is smaller. The pantry gets less. But the families with children come back, some of them for the first time in years, and the fry is quieter and ends earlier, and something about it is more like Lent. {@maintenance} is unconvinced and says the parish will feel it in the poor box.

choices.label: Say nothing at the council, and work the fryer yourself every Friday of Lent
choices.outcome: You put on an apron. The dispute continues without you and resolves itself in the way disputes do when the priest is standing in the kitchen with a basket of cod; nobody wants to be the one who walked out on him. The beer comes back in week three by a vote you were not at. You have burned your forearm and learned every Knight's name, and the fry is the best-attended in years, and none of that was administration.

events.title: The Church Up the Road
events.body: {@parishioner} asks to see you, and it is to tell you, out of courtesy, that the family is leaving. Not the faith; the parish. They have been going to the nondenominational church up the road on Saturday nights, the one in the former hardware store with the band and the parking attendants, and the children love it, and the wife has found a women's group there that she says has done more for her in three months than {parish} did in eleven years. There is a pastor there who knows her name. There is coffee. He says it without anger. He says the children asked why the priest never talks to them, and that he did not have an answer, and that he does not blame you, because you are one man with four Masses. He has come to say this in person because his mother, who is still at the 8:00, would want him to. He would also like to know, and this is the real question, whether he is doing something wrong. He was baptized here. He was married here. He is asking a priest for permission to leave, and does not know that is what he is asking.
events.flavorPrompt: A decent man leaving for a place that knows his name. No polemic against the other church. The Eucharist is the argument, if there is one, and it may not be enough.

choices.label: Tell him what he will not have up the road, plainly, and that the door stays open
choices.outcome: You do not argue about the band. You say one thing: that whatever they have up the road, and it is a great deal, they do not have the Eucharist, and that he does, and that it is the only argument you have and it is the only one that matters. He is quiet. He goes anyway. Eighteen months later the wife comes back alone to the Saturday 5:00, and then with the youngest, and then he comes to Easter, and stands at the back.

choices.label: Ask him what {parish} should have done, and write it down in front of him
choices.outcome: He is surprised to be asked and then has a list: nobody greeted them for a year, the youth group met twice, the homilies were about nothing. You write it down. It is a fair list. He leaves anyway, but he shakes your hand, and you take the list to {@pastor}, who reads it and says the family was never very involved. Six months later there is a greeter ministry at the 11:00, which is yours, which is not nothing, and is not enough.

choices.label: Tell him he is not doing anything wrong, and that God is up the road too
choices.outcome: You say it because it is nearly true and because it is what he came for. He is grateful. He leaves at peace. His mother at the 8:00 asks you the following week what you said to him and you tell her, and she says nothing for a while and then says that a priest should have fought harder, and goes back to her pew. You have been kind. You are not sure you have been a priest.

events.title: In Loving Memory
events.body: The donor comes to you because {@pastor} has stopped taking his calls, which is a thing the donor says with a laugh that is not one. He is offering forty thousand dollars toward the new sound system, which the parish has needed for a decade and {@music_director} has begged for, on the condition that a plaque naming his late wife be installed on the ambo. On the ambo. Not in the vestibule with the others; on the front of the ambo, where the Gospel is read, in brass, at a size he has specified in a drawing. {@pastor}'s position, relayed by {@secretary}, is that the ambo is not for sale and that the man knows it and is testing the new priest. {@music_director}'s position is that he would install the plaque himself with his own hands. The finance council has heard about the offer and is split. The donor gives a fifth of the collection in a good year and he is standing in your office with a drawing, and he is also a widower who misses his wife and does not know how else to say so. He says he would like an answer before the anniversary of her death, which is next month.
events.flavorPrompt: Money with a condition, grief underneath it. Neither the pastor nor the donor is simply right. The brass on the ambo is the image.

choices.label: Offer him the sound system named for her in the bulletin and on a plaque by the choir loft, and the ambo left alone
choices.outcome: You draw it for him: a plaque at the base of the loft stairs, where the singers pass it every Sunday, and a line in the bulletin every Easter and Christmas. You say the ambo belongs to the Word and that she would not have wanted to be in front of it. He is offended for ten minutes and moved for the rest of the meeting. The check is for thirty-five thousand, not forty, which is his way of registering the difference. {@music_director} has his system.

choices.label: Tell him the ambo is not for sale, and that the parish will find the money elsewhere
choices.outcome: You say it as {@pastor} would have and you say it more gently than he would have, and it makes no difference. The donor leaves. His envelope the following Sunday is empty, and the one after, and the finance council meets about it. {@music_director} does not get his sound system. {@pastor} says you did the right thing in a voice that suggests he had hoped you would find another one.

choices.label: Take the forty thousand and put the plaque on the ambo; it is brass, not doctrine
choices.outcome: You persuade {@pastor} that the ambo has had worse things on it than a widow's name, and he signs, because he is tired of the calls. The system is installed by Advent and the parish can hear the readings for the first time in years. The plaque is small and everyone sees it. Two priests of the deanery mention it. {@bishop}, at confirmation, glances at it and says nothing. The donor gives a quarter of the collection now, and knows it.

events.title: After the Youth Group
events.body: He waits until the others have gone. He is seventeen, a senior, an altar server since the fourth grade, the kind of boy the parish has already decided things about. He asks whether he can ask you something and then asks how you knew. Not whether he should be a priest; how you knew. He has told no one. His parents have plans for him that involve a university and, his father hopes, engineering, and his mother hopes, a wife. He has looked at the seminary's website and closed it. He has heard the things people say about the priesthood now, all of them, and he has decided he would rather hear it from you, because you are the youngest priest he has met and, he says, you seem normal. It is nine-fifteen on a Wednesday in the parish hall with the chairs half stacked. You remember being asked, or not being asked, at his age. You remember what the man who answered you said, or did not say, and what it cost, and what it made. The boy is waiting, and whatever you say next he will remember at forty.
events.flavorPrompt: A vocation seed. The priest's own story is in the room without being told. No recruitment, no discouragement; honesty at seventeen's scale.

choices.label: Tell him the truth, all of it: how you knew, what it cost, what it is like on a Tuesday
choices.outcome: You tell him about the moment, and about the years of not being sure after it, and about the rectory at nine o'clock, and about the seal and the hospital at three in the morning, and about the Vigil. You do not tell him what to do. He listens without moving. He says thank you and goes home. He does not mention it again for a year, and then he asks you to take him to the discernment weekend, and you do.

choices.label: Give him {@vocation_director}'s number and offer to make the call with him
choices.outcome: You say the diocese has a priest whose whole job is this question, and that he is good at it, and you make the call from the hall with the boy beside you. {@vocation_director} is pleased and says so to the chancery, where a vicar who sends names is noted. The boy goes to the retreat in the spring. He is one name on a list now. You were the one who could have been more than that, and chose the office instead.

choices.label: Tell him to go to the university, live, and ask again at twenty-two
choices.outcome: You say it because you believe it, or because you are tired, and you cannot tell which: go, study, date someone, break a heart or have one broken, and if it is still there at twenty-two it is real. He is disappointed and relieved. He goes to the university. He does not come back to the question, or he does, somewhere you are not. His mother thanks you at Christmas for talking sense to him. {@vocation_director}, who has heard, does not.

events.title: The Book
events.body: It takes {@pastor} four months to notice that you are good at this, and one week to act on it. The sacramental calendar, which has been {@secretary}'s and before her the previous secretary's and before that a system of index cards nobody could read, is now yours: every baptism, wedding, quinceañera, funeral, First Communion, and confirmation for the year, the preparation for each, the registers, the certificates, the letters of freedom, the dispensations, the bookings for the hall. He hands it to you at breakfast with a folder and the words: you have a gift. {@secretary} has been told, and has received the news as a demotion, which it is. {@dre} would like the First Communion dates moved and has been waiting a year to be allowed to ask. The finance council chair has already asked whether, since you are doing the book, you would sit on the building committee, which meets Tuesdays, and the deanery has heard there is a vicar at {parish} who can run a calendar, and there is a diocesan committee on sacramental records that meets quarterly and has a vacancy. It is Thursday. The folder is four inches thick and the first wedding in it is Saturday.
events.flavorPrompt: The cost of high Administration: competence rewarded with more of the same. Committees arrive like weather.

choices.label: Take the book, fix it, and decline every committee
choices.outcome: You rebuild the calendar in a month and {@dre} gets her dates, and the letters go out on time for the first time in living memory, and {@secretary} comes around slowly. You say no to the building committee and no to the deanery, politely, twice. {@pastor} has never had a vicar who could do this and finds he cannot spare you, which he says to {@vicar_general} as praise, and which the chancery hears as a reason to leave you where you are.

choices.label: Take the book and the committees; a man who is useful is a man who is seen
choices.outcome: The book, the building committee, the diocesan records committee. By spring you are known at the chancery as the vicar who can be given things. The calendar is good. The hospital sees you less. {@pastor} notices you are out three nights a week and says nothing; he gave you the book. When the assignment board meets, your name is on a list of men who are needed exactly where they are, which is a compliment with a floor under it.

choices.label: Keep the book in {@secretary}'s hands, fix the system with her, and let her keep the title
choices.outcome: You tell {@pastor} you will oversee it and that {@secretary} will run it, and you spend a month of afternoons at her desk building something she can use. She is suspicious and then, when she sees that you meant it, formidable. The calendar works. She tells the deanery secretaries, who tell their pastors, that the vicar at {parish} is a gentleman. You have given away the credit and kept the parish's memory intact. Nobody at the chancery knows your name for it.
